messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Unemployed
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory/Mechanical: Motorcycle noise, Auditory (Language): Shouting in Arabic, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Avoid Night: Going out at night or being outside after dark, Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
  Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Jasmine's Story

Jasmine was nineteen when she married Marcus, a decision that had felt like the right one at the time—a commitment to someone who made her feel seen. She had been working part-time at a coffee shop near campus, saving money, imagining a future that felt manageable and warm. That was before the night in October when everything fractured into something unrecognizable.

She had been walking home from a late shift, cutting through the parking garage as she always did. A man had been waiting. She had not seen his face clearly in the darkness, but she heard his voice—sharp, commanding, in Arabic, a language she did not understand but that seemed to carry a violence of its own. He had smelled of alcohol, thick and suffocating. There had been the sound of his motorcycle outside the garage afterward, the engine roaring as he fled, a sound that had etched itself into her nervous system with such precision that months later, any motorcycle in the distance would send her body into a state of alert that felt like drowning while standing still.

In the weeks that followed, Jasmine had tried to return to work. But the coffee shop, with its open layout and glass doors, had begun to feel indefensible. She found herself listening constantly for sounds—the scrape of a chair, the jingle of keys—interpreting each one as a potential threat. One afternoon, a customer had shouted in Arabic to his friend across the café, and Jasmine had frozen, her hands shaking so badly that she dropped an entire tray of cups. She had not returned after that shift. Marcus had said it was okay, that he could support them both, but the loss of that small independence had added another weight to the ones already pressing down on her chest.

The nights became impossible. She could not bring herself to go outside after dark. The thought of being in the open, where someone could approach from behind, made her skin crawl. She had taken to checking behind her constantly, even in their apartment, even in rooms she had just looked at moments before. The checking never brought relief, only a temporary pause before the fear crept back in. Marcus had noticed her doing it—spinning around, peering into shadows—and she could see the worry in his eyes, the unspoken question about whether she was becoming someone he did not recognize. She was becoming someone she did not recognize.

Certain dates had become unbearable. The anniversary of the assault approached like a storm she could see on the horizon, and the dread began weeks in advance. She had started avoiding that entire week in October, staying in bed, refusing to engage with the world. The smell of alcohol—on Marcus's breath after he came home from seeing friends, in the air at a grocery store—would send her spiraling backward into that garage, the sensations returning with a vividness that made her question whether she was remembering or reliving.

What frightened her most was not just the fear itself, but what she had come to believe about herself. She had once been someone who worked, who moved through the world with a kind of confidence that now felt like a fantasy she had invented. She found herself unable to look at her own body without feeling a deep revulsion, as though her skin had become a thing that had betrayed her. She would shower with her eyes closed, dress without mirrors. When she thought about what had happened, she did not just see it—she heard the Arabic words again, smelled the alcohol, felt the weight of a hand she could not escape. The memories arrived without warning, triggered by the smallest sensory echo, and she had no defense against them.

What haunted her most, though, was the conviction that someone else—someone braver, someone stronger—would have fought back, would have stopped it from happening. The world, she had come to believe, was not a place where safety existed. It was a place where violence waited in parking garages and in the voices of strangers, and she was not capable of surviving it the way other people might.

It was Marcus who finally insisted she see someone. He had found her one morning sitting on the bathroom floor, unable to move, and something in his face—fear mixed with helplessness—had broken through her isolation enough to make her agree. She had called a therapist that afternoon, her hands trembling as she dialed, terrified of what it would mean to speak it all aloud, but more terrified of the alternative: a life spent checking behind her, avoiding her own body, waiting for the next sound that would send her back to that garage.
